hints: Notice the input is $2.0 \text{ kW} = 2000 \text{ W}$ of electrical power, while the useful output is the gain in gravitational potential energy of $16 \text{ kg}$ lifted $7.0 \text{ m}$ every second.
Connect mass per second to power using $P_{out} = mgh/t$, with $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $h = 7.0 \text{ m}$.
Calculate $P_{out}$ in watts, check it is near $1100 \text{ W}$, then use $\text{efficiency} = P_{out}/P_{in}$ and convert to a percentage to compare with $1.8\%$, $5.6\%$, $22\%$ and $55\%$.
walkthrough: Identify input power and useful output. Input $P_{in} = 2.0 \text{ kW} = 2000 \text{ W}$. Useful energy per second is gravitational potential energy $mgh$.
State the efficiency rule: $\text{efficiency} = \text{useful power output} / \text{total power input}$.
Calculate useful power output for $m = 16 \text{ kg}$ lifted in $t = 1 \text{ s}$ through $h = 7.0 \text{ m}$: $P_{out} = mgh/t = 16 \times 9.81 \times 7.0 / 1$.
Divide by input and convert to percentage: $\text{efficiency} = 1098.7 / 2000 = 0.549$, about $55\%$. Units cancel $\text{W}/\text{W}$, leaving a dimensionless ratio.

options.A: Too small by a factor of about 30. It may come from an error in converting $2.0 \text{ kW}$ to watts or in forming the ratio.
options.B: Too small by a factor of about 10. It may come from using $16 \text{ kg}$ as weight in newtons instead of multiplying by $g$.
options.C: Too small. It may come from using $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ incorrectly combined with an arithmetic error, since the correct useful power is about $1100 \text{ W}$.
options.D: Useful output power $mgh/t$ is about $1100 \text{ W}$, so efficiency is about $1100/2000 = 0.55 = 55\%$.
